theory.heading: Botanical groups, not hardness ratings
theory.body: Hardwood and softwood are botanical categories based on the type of tree the timber comes from. Hardwood usually comes from flowering trees, while softwood usually comes from cone-bearing trees. The names do not guarantee how hard, heavy or strong a piece of timber will be. Some hardwoods are relatively soft, and some softwoods are firm and durable. This means students should not judge a timber only from its category name. Use hardwood and softwood as classification words, then consider the actual properties of the material.

theory.heading: Pine in the Footstool project
theory.body: Pine is identified as the timber used for the Footstool project. Pine belongs to the softwood botanical group, but this label does not describe every property that matters during practical work. Individual pieces may differ in grain pattern, density, knots, surface condition or other visible features. The fact that pine is a softwood does not mean students may assume that every piece will behave in exactly the same way. Teacher-provided project requirements and approved material information guide the actual selection and use of timber.

theory.heading: Choose using relevant properties
theory.body: Material choice involves matching useful properties to the project requirements. A student might consider workability, appearance, grain, density, condition and suitability for the intended purpose. These factors provide more useful evidence than simply choosing hardwood because it sounds stronger or rejecting softwood because it sounds weak. Before making a judgement, identify the botanical category, observe the relevant properties and compare them with the teacher-provided requirements. Current school SOPs and teacher directions control all actual workshop activity. When material information is unclear, pause and ask rather than making an unsupported assumption.

questions.question: What do the words hardwood and softwood mainly describe?
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Hardwood and softwood are botanical categories based on the type of tree.
questions.retryFeedback: Review Botanical groups, not hardness ratings and focus on what the two terms classify.

questions.question: Why can the term hardwood be misleading?
choices: Some hardwoods can be relatively soft
The term only describes timber colour
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. The botanical label hardwood does not guarantee that the timber is physically hard.
questions.retryFeedback: Return to Botanical groups, not hardness ratings and examine why the category name is not a hardness rating.

questions.question: Which statement about softwoods is accurate?
choices: They are always softer than hardwoods
Some can be firm and durable
They cannot be used for projects
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Softwood is a botanical category, and some softwoods can be firm and durable.
questions.retryFeedback: Re-read Botanical groups, not hardness ratings and find the example that challenges a simple assumption about softwood.

questions.question: Which botanical group does pine belong to?
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Pine belongs to the softwood botanical group.
questions.retryFeedback: Review Pine in the Footstool project and identify the category given for pine.

questions.question: What timber is identified for the Footstool project?
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Pine is identified as the timber used for the Footstool project.
questions.retryFeedback: Return to Pine in the Footstool project and focus on the named project material.

questions.question: Why should students inspect individual pieces of pine?
choices: Every piece must have a different botanical category
Pieces may differ in grain, density, knots or condition
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Individual pieces can vary in visible features and material properties.
questions.retryFeedback: Re-read Pine in the Footstool project and identify the ways pieces of the same timber may differ.

questions.question: What should guide the actual selection and use of timber?
choices: A guess based on the category name
Teacher-provided requirements and approved material information
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Project requirements and approved material information guide selection and use.
questions.retryFeedback: Review the final sentence of Pine in the Footstool project and focus on what controls material decisions.

questions.question: Which factor is useful when judging material suitability?
choices: A claim that all hardwood is stronger
The material nearest to the bench
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Workability and condition are relevant properties when considering suitability.
questions.retryFeedback: Return to Choose using relevant properties and identify the material factors listed there.

questions.question: Why is choosing hardwood only because it sounds stronger a weak decision?
choices: Hardwood is not a botanical term
All hardwood is unsuitable for projects
The category name alone does not prove suitable properties
Softwood and hardwood are identical materials
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. A botanical label alone does not show whether the material meets the project requirements.
questions.retryFeedback: Re-read Choose using relevant properties and focus on why category names provide limited evidence.

questions.question: What should a student do when material information is unclear?
choices: Make an assumption from the name
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Pausing and asking prevents unsupported assumptions about the material.
questions.retryFeedback: Review the final sentence of Choose using relevant properties and identify the response to uncertainty.

written.prompt: Explain why calling pine a softwood does not fully describe whether a piece is suitable for the Footstool project. Include two relevant properties that should also be considered.
written.sentenceStarter: Pine is classified as a softwood because ___. This does not fully describe its suitability because students must also consider ___ and ___.
written.example: Pine is classified as a softwood because it comes from a cone-bearing tree group. This does not fully describe its suitability because students must also consider properties such as grain and condition, together with the project requirements.
